records.artists: Lewis Wandin-Bursill (Wurundjeri artist), who developed the Woi-wurrung language and etched designs on the seating, drawing on the diamond motif of his ancestor William Barak; a Wurundjeri Elder (name not given) provided the manna gum leaf sketch

records.summary: A ceremonial gathering space within Melbourne's new City Square, co-designed by Greenshoot Consulting with Wurundjeri Elders. A central circular granite paved area has Woi-wurrung language set into the ground plane, a semi-circular granite seat etched with a diamond motif, and a rotating, lockable bronze Smoking Ceremony Dish on a stone plinth. Planting was selected in consultation with Wurundjeri Elders. The space supports formal ceremony and informal yarning.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how a ceremonial element can be added to an already resolved public realm while meeting operational constraints such as circulation, train station operations and smoke management. The lockable, rotating dish and the use of Elder-authored motifs are useful references for durable, culturally authored detailing.
records.description: The project is a ceremonial gathering place within Melbourne's new City Square, co-designed by Greenshoot Consulting with Wurundjeri Elders. It was commissioned after the square's design documentation was complete, so it had to fit into a resolved public realm. It sits centrally, keeps pedestrian movement and event flexibility, and needed endorsement from Traditional Owners, State Government, City of Melbourne and MTM. Early coordination dealt with circulation, train station operations and smoke management. The main element is a bronze Smoking Ceremony Dish on a granite plinth sourced from Country. The dish is rotating and lockable, balancing safety, durability and ceremonial expression. A manna gum leaf motif is embossed on the dish and etched into the plinth, taken from a sketch by a Wurundjeri Elder. A pattern inside the dish references the manna gum flower. Woi-wurrung language is set into a bespoke circular paving pattern that differs from the rest of the plaza. Semi-circular granite seating carries etched artwork by a Wurundjeri artist, drawing on William Barak's diamond motif. Planting was selected in consultation with Wurundjeri Elders, and interpretive signage supports public learning. The bronze is designed to patinate with use and touch. The space accommodates formal ceremony and informal yarning.

records.summary: A public art display in an inner Melbourne streetscape showing a large illuminated portrait panel of Aunty Annie Borate (as written on the panel), set into a concrete and metal service structure beside a heritage red brick building. The panel reads 'My name is Aunty Annie' with a line of First Peoples language and a green diamond pattern background. A small plaque beside it appears to be titled 'Celebrating Wurundjeri Women'. A group is gathered for a guided tour.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how a utilitarian piece of street infrastructure can carry a named First Peoples woman, language and pattern, making people visible in the city centre.
records.description: The photo shows a street corner in Melbourne's central city, with a red brick heritage building with cream rendered detailing on the left and high-rise towers behind. A concrete and metal structure topped by a ventilation stack has been fitted with a large framed display panel. The panel has a green background with a pale diamond pattern. It carries the text 'My name is Aunty Annie', a line in First Peoples language, and a black and white archival-style portrait of a woman. Smaller text curves around the portrait and includes 'Aunty Annie Borate' and 'I will be strong, I am strong'. A small plaque to the left of the panel appears to read 'Celebrating Wurundjeri Women', though it is hard to read in the photo. A group of people stands in front of the panel, apparently on a guided walk or tour, with a speaker facing them. The Instagram page text gave no caption, so designers, artists, date, client and Traditional Owner involvement are not confirmed from this material.

records.location_text: Queen & Collins, 376-390 Collins Street, Melbourne VIC

records.awards: 2023 Good Design Award, Built Environment Installation Design
records.summary: A ceremonial fire dish installed in 2023 as part of the Queen & Collins redevelopment in Naarm/Melbourne. It was co-designed by Greenshoot Consulting through engagement with Wurundjeri Traditional Owners. Bronze etchings in the dish represent the topography and precolonial waterways of central Melbourne, and nearby significant First Peoples landmarks are shown in an embedded wayfinding device. The dish sits in a paved court with granite and bronze text inscriptions.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how a small, object-scale element in a commercial redevelopment can carry Country, waterways and landmarks through etched mapping and wayfinding. It also shows co-design with Traditional Owners producing an award-recognised outcome.
records.description: The ceremonial fire dish was originally installed in 2023 as part of the Queen & Collins redevelopment in Naarm/Melbourne. Greenshoot Consulting co-designed it through its engagement with Wurundjeri Traditional Owners. It won the 2023 Good Design Award for Built Environment Installation Design. The bronze etchings within the dish represent the topography and precolonial waterways of the centre of Naarm/Melbourne. Significant First Peoples landmarks close to the project site are also featured in the embedded wayfinding device. The project was again open to visitors as part of Open House Melbourne. The photo shows the bronze dish with etched contour and waterway lines, set beside a granite surface with bronze inscriptions including 'Site of first recorded Aboriginal burial' and a line referring to a place for reflection. Eucalyptus foliage and dark stones sit beside the dish, and brick paving surrounds the court. The second image is a render of the wider redevelopment, showing towers, a playing field and rooftop planting.

records.location_text: Northcote Aquatic and Recreation Centre, 180 Victoria Road, Northcote VIC
records.first_peoples_collaborators: Aunty Joy Murphy (Wurundjeri Elder), Uncle Colin Hunter (Wurundjeri), Craig Murphy (Wurundjeri), Greenshoot Consulting (cultural codesign), Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation (Traditional Owner group, consulted on facility and landscape design)
records.other_team: Brett Diprose, Warren and Mahoney (project architect); Greenaway Architects (assisted Traditional Owner consultation); Kane Constructions (builder); Taylor Thomson Whitting (structural and civil engineer); Arup (environmental consultant); Crackerjack Consulting Engineers (aquatic design); Introba (building services); Normark Landscapes (landscape contractor); Rubner (timber structure); Klay Tiles
records.summary: Cultural codesign for the new Northcote Aquatic and Recreation Centre in Northcote, Victoria, designed by WAM. Greenshoot Consulting worked with Wurundjeri Elders to embed three interventions: a three by five metre Sacred Kingfisher in flight on the Victoria Road facade, made from coloured metal rods; water ribbon patterning in the splash pad; and a cultural gathering space for yarning and cultural practice.
records.why_it_matters: It shows Elders directing how cultural knowledge is translated into a facade artwork, floor patterning and a gathering space within a public aquatic centre. The kingfisher links Wurundjeri knowledge of pristine waterways to the building's sustainability aims.
records.description: The Northcote Aquatic and Recreation Centre was delivered during Treaty discussions, with the aim of setting a benchmark in culturally responsive design. Greenshoot Consulting codesigned interventions with Aunty Joy Murphy, Uncle Colin Hunter and Craig Murphy (Wurundjeri), working with the lead design team, WAM. The Elders directed how cultural knowledge was reflected in the design. Three elements resulted. First, a Sacred Kingfisher on the main street facade, drawn from Wurundjeri knowledge that the kingfisher only returns to pristine waterways. It represents the environmental initiatives in the building and the pool water filtration systems. The bird is formed from metal rods of three lengths, giving depth and casting shadows that change through the day on the western facade. The rods are teal blue, black and ochre, the kingfisher's main colours. The bird is shown in flight to reflect its seasonal migratory nature. The installation is three metres high and five metres wide. Second, water ribbon inspired patterning in the water play splash pad, reflecting water systems near the site. Third, a cultural gathering space for yarning and cultural practice, returning a practice that existed in the region before colonisation. In the courtyard, a boulder sits among curved timber seats on exposed aggregate paving.

records.name: Mission Whitten Oval Yarning Circle
records.location_text: Mission Whitten Oval (Whitten Oval), Footscray VIC
records.country_to: Kulin Nation (Wurundjeri, Bunurong and Boon Wurrung Traditional Owners named for the wider Whitten Oval redevelopment; Wurundjeri man Thane Garvey led the opening smoking ceremony)
records.architect: Jefa Greenaway (Wailwan/Kamilaroi man), in partnership with Greenshoot Consulting
records.first_peoples_collaborators: Greenshoot Consulting (cultural and historical mapping, Traditional Owner engagement); Jefa Greenaway (Wailwan/Kamilaroi); Traditional Owners of the land on which the Club resides (consulted); Wurundjeri, Bunurong and Boon Wurrung Elders (workshops for the wider redevelopment); Thane Garvey (Wurundjeri man, led the smoking ceremony)
records.other_team: Populous (architect and design management, Whitten Oval redevelopment); Urbis (landscape architect, Whitten Oval redevelopment); Aurecon (structural, civil and services engineering, redevelopment); ADCO Constructions (main works builder, redevelopment)
records.summary: The Mission Whitten Oval Yarning Circle is an outdoor gathering space for players and staff at the Western Bulldogs' home ground in Footscray, Melbourne. It was created during the Oval's redevelopment, with Greenshoot Consulting and Jefa Greenaway engaged to guide cultural design. Key moves include a bluestone floor referencing the former quarry, a central map of Blue Lake with bronze inlays of First Nations sites, a metal strip for the Maribyrnong River, and boomerang-form hardwood posts and seating.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how Traditional Owner consultation can lead to a dedicated, culturally safe gathering space inside a sporting facility, with ceremony such as Welcome to Country built into the brief. The material, map and form choices tie the design to local geology, waterways and history. The engagement was staged: desktop research on site and club history, preliminary cultural themes, then Elder workshops across several Traditional Owner groups. This is a useful model for multi-group consultation on a sporting venue.
records.description: The Western Bulldogs Football Club announced the opening of the Mission Whitten Oval Yarning Circle on 18 May 2026. Consultation with the Traditional Owners of the land on which the Club resides highlighted the need for dedicated outdoor spaces where players and staff can gather and yarn. These spaces were identified as important for connection, support networks and cultural safety across the Club. As part of the recent redevelopment of Mission Whitten Oval, the Club engaged Greenshoot Consulting in partnership with Jefa Greenaway to identify ways the facility could recognise and celebrate the First Nations community. The oval sits on the traditional, unceded lands of the Woiwurrung Wurundjeri and Boon wurrung language groups of the Kulin Nation. The Club saw the redevelopment as an opportunity to amplify First Peoples' connection to the site and to set a benchmark in First Peoples engagement and design. Greenshoot carried out cultural and historical mapping, researching the site's pre-colonisation history, important First Peoples figures in the Club and moments in its recent history. It then prepared documentation setting out preliminary cultural themes to inform consultation with Wurundjeri, Bunurong and Boon Wurrung stakeholders. Greenshoot facilitated workshops with Elders from the three Traditional Owner groups, and with key First Peoples stakeholders, to expand on these themes and explore the site using its First Peoples Design Consultation Pillars. The circle also provides space for Traditional Owners to hold ceremonies such as Welcome to Country for new players and staff, as well as the public. The floor is bluestone, acknowledging that Whitten Oval sits on a former bluestone quarry. A map at the centre is shaped to represent Blue Lake, the initial name for the Footscray area. It carries an inscription of the Blue Lake area and bronze inlays marking significant local First Nations sites. A metal strip running through the ground represents the Maribyrnong River and the importance of waterways. Upright hardwood posts reference the boomerang form, which is repeated in the seating. The circle was officially opened during Sir Doug Nicholls Round, with the whole Club taking part in a smoking ceremony led by Wurundjeri man Thane Garvey.

records.name: Marvel Stadium Upgrade
records.first_peoples_collaborators: Greenshoot Consulting (First Peoples engagement and codesign); Wurundjeri Elders including Uncle Colin Hunter Jnr and Aunty Joy Murphy Wandin; Elders representing the three Traditional Owner groups
records.summary: The Marvel Stadium upgrade in Melbourne, led by architect Grimshaw for Development Victoria and completed in 2022, embedded First Peoples cultural expression in the new precinct. Greenshoot Consulting engaged Elders from the three Traditional Owner groups and codesigned elements with Wurundjeri Elders. These include ground plane treatment at the new entry points, column design within those entries, and a ceiling design at the City Edge location, with further art opportunities for First Peoples artists identified.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how a structured engagement program can turn Elders' priorities into specific architectural and landscape elements on a large commercial precinct. The ceiling and column elements are useful references for embedding cultural expression in major built fabric, with art commissions left open for First Peoples artists.
records.description:
The Marvel Stadium upgrade, completed in 2022, created an opportunity to embed First Peoples-led design and cultural expression into the new precinct. The client was Development Victoria and the lead architect was Grimshaw. Greenshoot Consulting ran a program of engagement with Elders representing the three Traditional Owner groups, using Greenshoot's First Peoples Design Consultation Pillars. This allowed opportunities identified by Traditional Owners to be mapped across Narrative, Design and Activation domains, to support the embedding of Traditional Owner knowledge and culture in the redevelopment. Through engagement with Wurundjeri Elders, including Uncle Colin Hunter Jnr and Aunty Joy Murphy Wandin, Greenshoot codesigned various elements within the architecture and landscape. These opportunities developed within the City Edge and Town Square locations: the ground plane treatment at the new entry points, column design within those entry points, and a ceiling design at the City Edge location. The site photo shows a perforated metal ceiling with a large dark figure formed by the perforation pattern, with a line of linked points and light fittings across it. Wurundjeri Elders also identified further art opportunities for First Peoples artists within the column design, to tell stories of Wurundjeri culture and Country.

Additional site photos of the public concourse and forecourt show further pattern and paving elements. A ceiling of perforated, warm-toned panels carries a dark dot pattern forming a large irregular shape, with fine lines and small lights connecting points across it, and linear light fittings set into the panels. On the concourse and plaza, large white oval rings of varying size are laid over grey concrete with overlapping tonal zones and fields of circular dots. Close-up photos of sandstone-coloured paving show shallow etched or inlaid motifs: a snake or eel-like form, a eucalypt branch with a bud and a metal blossom inlay, flowing leaf-like shapes, and a round metal inlay with fine radiating lines. A wider view shows the ring pattern on an open forecourt with the Melbourne CBD and Southern Cross Station roofs behind. The photos came without credits, and they do not state the purpose, meaning or authorship of these motifs or whether they form part of the Wurundjeri codesigned elements described above. They are recorded here as visual references.
